CODE-004 describes fee asymmetry from Step 4 unwind selling absolute pump output creating systematic sUSDS deficit. ECON-003 describes pump/unwind costs exceeding discount rate. ECON-005 describes payment based on theoretical yield not actual tokens received. All three share the same root cause: the pump/unwind flow creates a systematic value leak because the unwind step does not account for fees/slippage consumed during the pump step, and payment is calculated on theoretical rather than realized amounts. These are different manifestations of the same economic asymmetry.

findings.title: Residual phUSD delta silently dropped in _settleResidualDelta causes ClaimArbitrage DoS
findings.description: _settleResidualDelta(phUSD) silently returns at line 335 when no stableToUSDCPool[phUSD] is configured and phUSD != sUSDS. If any residual negative phUSD delta exists from the pump/unwind (which is common due to AMM rounding), it remains unsettled. The PoolManager enforces a zero-delta invariant and reverts the entire execute() transaction. This renders ClaimArbitrage non-functional for any scenario producing even a dust-level residual phUSD delta.
findings.impact: ClaimArbitrage becomes permanently DoSed whenever a residual phUSD delta exists after unwind. The silent return at line 335 masks the root cause, making diagnosis difficult. Yield distribution through ClaimArbitrage is blocked.
findings.recommendation: Either configure stableToUSDCPool[phUSD] to provide a settlement path, add a fallback settlement through the phUSD/sUSDS pool, or at minimum revert with a descriptive error instead of silently returning.

findings.title: claim() reverts on any paused token while calculateClaimAmount() skips them -- global DoS on yield claiming
findings.description: claim() at line 589 reverts with TokenIsPaused() for ANY paused token in the iteration loop. calculateClaimAmount() at line 803 uses 'continue' to skip paused tokens. This inconsistency means: (1) pausing a single low-value token blocks ALL claims across ALL strategies; (2) calculateClaimAmount() returns misleading values that cannot be claimed; (3) TOCTOU: off-chain callers (including ClaimArbitrage bot) read calculateClaimAmount() which reports claimable yield, then claim() reverts because it encounters the paused token. The fix for the claim/calculate inconsistency eliminates both the DoS and the TOCTOU manifestation.
findings.impact: Pausing a single token (expected admin behavior during depeg events) prevents claiming yield from ALL strategies. calculateClaimAmount() returns misleading amounts. Blocks ClaimArbitrage and all individual claimers.
findings.recommendation: Change claim() to skip paused tokens with 'continue' (matching calculateClaimAmount() behavior). If all-or-nothing semantics are intentional, update calculateClaimAmount() to also revert on paused tokens.

findings.title: ClaimArbitrage Steps 5/6/7 internal swaps use no slippage protection, enabling sandwich attacks
findings.description: All stablecoin conversion swaps (Steps 5/6/7) use type(uint160).min+1 or type(uint160).max-1 as sqrtPriceLimitX96 -- effectively zero slippage protection. While the pump step (Step 3) and unwind step (Step 4) have configurable pumpPriceLimit/unwindPriceLimit parameters, the stablecoin-to-USDC conversion and profit-to-WETH conversion swaps have no bounds. MEV bots can sandwich these swaps to extract value from the profitable margin.
findings.impact: MEV bots can sandwich the execute() transaction, manipulating prices in the stable-to-USDC and USDC-to-WETH pools. The NoProfit check prevents total loss but sandwich attacks extract value from the profit margin. Reduces effective discount rate for legitimate arbitrageurs.
findings.recommendation: Add slippage limit parameters to ExecuteParams for each swap step. Extend the pumpPriceLimit/unwindPriceLimit pattern to all internal swaps.

findings.title: Step 4 unwind sells absolute pump output -- fee asymmetry creates systematic sUSDS deficit and theoretical-vs-actual yield mismatch
findings.description: Three related manifestations of a single root cause: (1) CODE-004: The Step 4 unwind sells the absolute pump output amount without accounting for fees consumed during the pump step. The pump swaps phUSD->sUSDS, paying pool fees. The unwind then tries to sell the exact same sUSDS amount back, but the net return is less than the original due to round-trip fees, creating a systematic sUSDS deficit. (2) ECON-003: The combined pump/unwind costs (2x pool fees + price impact) may exceed the discount rate that makes arbitrage profitable, causing execute() to revert with NoProfit or succeed with negligible profit. (3) ECON-005: Payment to Phlimbo is calculated based on theoretical yield (calculateClaimAmount) rather than actual tokens received after swap slippage, creating a mismatch between what the protocol pays out and what it receives.
findings.impact: Systematic value leak on every ClaimArbitrage execution. The protocol pays Phlimbo based on theoretical yield while receiving less due to round-trip swap fees. Over time this drains more value than intended. In extreme cases, the fee asymmetry makes arbitrage unprofitable, blocking yield distribution entirely.
findings.recommendation: Calculate unwind amount as (pump output - estimated fees) rather than absolute pump output. Base Phlimbo payment on actual tokens received post-swap rather than theoretical calculateClaimAmount(). Add profitability checks that account for round-trip swap costs.
findings.note: NEW FINDING - not previously tracked in any audit pass

findings.title: Stale USDC approval persists on SYA after claim() -- enables approval exhaustion attack
findings.description: After ClaimArbitrage calls SYA.claim(), a stale USDC approval remains on the SYA contract. The approval is set before the claim but not revoked after. An attacker can: (1) observe the stale approval via on-chain state, (2) call transferFrom to drain the remaining approved USDC from ClaimArbitrage, (3) repeat on each claim cycle. Additionally, there is a race condition between the off-chain calculateClaimAmount read and the on-chain claim execution -- if yield changes between these calls, the pre-calculated approval amount becomes stale, either reverting the transaction (approval too low) or leaving excess approval (approval too high).
findings.impact: Stale USDC approvals can be exploited to drain USDC from ClaimArbitrage. If the approval amount exceeds the actual claim cost, the difference remains approved and is extractable by any party. Repeated exploitation across claim cycles compounds the loss.
findings.recommendation: Reset USDC approval to 0 after each claim() call completes. Use approve(0) then approve(exactAmount) pattern, or use increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance. Consider using permit-based single-use approvals.
findings.note: NEW FINDING - combines approval lifecycle issues from both scanners

findings.title: Rounding loss in normalize/denormalize for 6-decimal tokens compounds over time
findings.description: Decimal truncation occurs when normalizing and denormalizing amounts for tokens with fewer than 18 decimals (e.g., USDC with 6 decimals). The rounding consistently favors claimers: fractions are truncated down during denormalization, meaning the protocol receives slightly less payment per claim than theoretically owed.
findings.impact: Systematic dust-level loss per claim transaction. While individually negligible, the loss compounds across thousands of claims. The protocol slowly leaks value in favor of claimers.
findings.recommendation: Round up (ceil) during denormalization rather than truncating, to favor the protocol. Alternatively, document this as accepted behavior and quantify maximum cumulative impact.
findings.note: Overlaps with existing L-01 from stable-yield-accumulator-01 audit. Severity may remain Low/QA.

findings.title: Static 1:1 exchange rate enables value extraction when phUSD trades above peg
findings.description: The protocol assumes a static 1:1 exchange rate between phUSD and USDS/USDC for payment calculations. When phUSD trades above peg (e.g., during high demand or after pump manipulation), claimers pay less in real value than the yield they receive. The discount is proportional to the deviation above peg. This creates a systematic arbitrage opportunity: buy phUSD below market rate through the claim mechanism whenever phUSD is above peg.
findings.impact: Direct value extraction from the protocol when phUSD trades above peg. Claimers receive yield priced at 1:1 while the market values phUSD higher. The protocol subsidizes the difference. Larger deviations above peg amplify the extraction.
findings.recommendation: Use an oracle-based exchange rate for phUSD rather than assuming 1:1. Alternatively, add a price band check that reverts claims when phUSD is significantly above peg.
findings.note: NEW FINDING - distinct from CODE-009 rounding issue despite both touching token math

findings.title: ETH-only profit distribution blocks non-payable contract callers from using ClaimArbitrage
findings.description: ClaimArbitrage distributes profit as native ETH via a low-level call. If the caller is a smart contract without a payable receive/fallback function, the ETH transfer fails and the entire execute() transaction reverts. This prevents contract-based callers (multisigs, DAOs, smart wallets, automated bots deployed as contracts) from participating in yield arbitrage.
findings.impact: Non-payable contract callers are completely excluded from ClaimArbitrage. This reduces the set of potential arbitrageurs, decreasing competition and potentially allowing fewer/larger extractors to capture yield arbitrage opportunities. Smart contract wallets (increasingly common) cannot use the protocol.
findings.recommendation: Add a WETH fallback: attempt ETH transfer, and if it fails, wrap to WETH and transfer the ERC-20 token instead. Alternatively, allow callers to specify a profit recipient address.

findings.title: Discount rate defaults to 0, creating silent deadlock where ClaimArbitrage is unprofitable
findings.description: If the discount rate is not explicitly configured or defaults to 0, claimers must pay 100% of yield value, making arbitrage mathematically unprofitable after accounting for gas and swap fees. The execute() call either reverts with NoProfit or produces zero profit. There is no warning or revert when discount rate is 0 -- the system silently becomes non-functional.
findings.impact: ClaimArbitrage cannot profitably execute with a 0 discount rate. Yield accumulates in SYA but cannot be distributed to Phlimbo stakers. The protocol's core yield distribution mechanism is silently deadlocked.
findings.recommendation: Add a minimum discount rate validation in setDiscountRate(). Revert or emit a warning if discount rate is set to 0. Consider initializing with a reasonable default (e.g., 1-5%).

findings.title: Phlimbo USDC approval exhaustion halts yield distribution permanently
findings.description: The USDC approval from ClaimArbitrage to Phlimbo (or SYA to Phlimbo) can be exhausted over successive claim cycles. Once the cumulative USDC transferred exceeds the initial approval, subsequent collectReward() calls revert with an insufficient allowance error. If the approval is not refreshed (no re-approval mechanism in the claim flow), yield distribution halts permanently until manual intervention.
findings.impact: Permanent halt of yield distribution once USDC approval is exhausted. All pending yield becomes unclaimable. Phlimbo stakers receive no rewards. Requires manual owner intervention to re-approve, during which yield continues to accumulate but cannot be distributed.
findings.recommendation: Use type(uint256).max approval (infinite approval) for the trusted Phlimbo contract, or implement approve-per-claim logic that sets exact approval before each collectReward() call. Add monitoring/alerting for low remaining approval.
findings.note: NEW FINDING - High severity due to permanent fund freezing without manual intervention

findings.title: Validation gap: _validateKnownStablesCoverage checks knownStables but not pool route existence
findings.description: _validateKnownStablesCoverage verifies that all SYA yield tokens are present in the knownStables array, but does not verify that a valid swap route (stableToUSDCPool mapping) exists for each known stable. A token can pass the coverage check but then fail at runtime during Step 5 swap because no pool route is configured. This creates a false sense of validation completeness.
findings.impact: ClaimArbitrage can pass all pre-execution validation checks but revert during actual execution when a swap route is missing. The validation provides incomplete coverage, giving operators false confidence that the configuration is correct.
findings.recommendation: Extend _validateKnownStablesCoverage to also verify that stableToUSDCPool[token] is set for each known stable (except sUSDS which has a direct path). Revert with a descriptive error if any pool route is missing.

reviewNotes: DEDUP-005 (stale USDC approval): Flagged for human review -- verify whether SYA.claim() consumes exact approval or leaves residual. If approval is set to exact calculateClaimAmount() result but actual claim uses less, the residual is exploitable.
DEDUP-006a (rounding loss): This overlaps with L-01 from stable-yield-accumulator-01. Consider keeping as QA only unless the new scanner found a novel escalation path.

DEDUP-006b (1:1 exchange rate): Verify this is not related to the rejected H-01 (spot price oracle manipulation). H-01 was rejected as 'intended behavior' but ECON-008 describes a different vector -- static exchange rate assumption, not spot price manipulation.

DEDUP-010 (approval exhaustion): Verify the exact approval flow. If ClaimArbitrage uses approve(exactAmount) per claim, this is not an issue. If it uses a one-time max approval, exhaustion is impossible. The finding severity depends on the actual approval pattern.

DEDUP-004 is a novel compound finding that was not present in any previous audit pass. It merges three scanner outputs into a single root-cause finding about pump/unwind fee asymmetry. Recommend prioritizing PoC development for this finding.
